newsitem.title: USA: Focusing trouble hits new Hubble camera.
newsitem.headline: Focusing trouble hits new Hubble camera.

text.p: A $105 million infrared camera fitted to the Hubble Space Telescope by space- walking astronauts last month was suffering focusing problems and may have a shorter lifetime than expected, NASA said on Wednesday.

A block of super-cold frozen nitrogen, used to cool the new instrument to -355 degrees Fahrenheit (-215 Celsius), was thawing faster than expected, distorting its thermos-like insulated container and ruining the focus of one of three infrared cameras, the space agency said in a news release.
The nitrogen was supposed to chill the infrared cameras for about four and a half years, but if it continues to thaw at the present rate, the supply could be exhausted in half that time.
The instrument's chief scientist, Rodger Thompson, of the University of Arizona, said the two working infrared cameras were returning excellent images.
The telescope's engineers were hopeful the problem would eventually correct itself, allowing them to complete their observations.
NASA said it would be several weeks or months until they know just how long the nitrogen will last. In the meantime, they were drawing up plans to complete the instrument's work in less time.

The Near-Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer, or NICMOS, was one of two new scientific instruments installed by the crew of the space shuttle Discovery during a $350 million orbital tune-up in February.
NICMOS is one of four instruments aboard the $2 billion orbiting observatory.
